title: Setting up your own Linux VM
lead: Install Rocky/Alma Linux or Ubuntu in VirtualBox, UTM or WSL, verify the download, take a snapshot and connect over SSH.
objectives: You pick the right tool for your computer (VirtualBox, UTM or WSL).
You verify the ISO with a SHA-256 checksum before installing.
You create a VM, take a snapshot and connect to it over SSH.

sections.title: Why your own VM?
body: Real skills come from a **real Linux**. A virtual machine (VM) is a complete computer inside your computer: you can break it, reinstall it and nothing on your real system is touched.

Pick the tool that fits your hardware: **VirtualBox** (Windows, Intel Mac, Linux), **UTM** (Apple Silicon Macs, needs an ARM64 ISO) or **WSL 2** (Windows 10/11, fastest to start, Ubuntu only). For distributions use **Rocky Linux 9 / AlmaLinux 9** (the RHEL family used in companies) and optionally **Ubuntu 24.04 LTS**.
sections.tip: Plan for 2 CPU cores, 4 GB RAM and 25 GB disk per VM.

sections.title: Download the ISO and verify it
body: Download the ISO only from the official site of the distribution (rockylinux.org, almalinux.org, ubuntu.com). Next to the ISO there is a **checksum** (SHA-256). Compute the checksum of your file and compare: if one character differs, the file is damaged or tampered with — download again.

commands.what: Computes the SHA-256 checksum of a file.
commands.where: On your host machine after the download.
commands.why: Proves the ISO is complete and unmodified.

sections.warn: Never install from an ISO whose checksum does not match, even if the installer starts.

sections.title: Create the VM and install
body: In VirtualBox/UTM create a new VM, attach the ISO and give it 2 CPUs, 4 GB RAM and 25 GB disk. Start it and follow the installer: choose your language, select the disk (automatic partitioning is fine), set a root password, **create a normal user and tick "administrator"** (this adds the user to the `wheel`/`sudo` group).
Choose the **Minimal** install first; you will add tools yourself. After the reboot remove the ISO and log in with your normal user. Finish with `cat /etc/os-release` to see which system you built.
On **WSL** this is one command in PowerShell (administrator): `wsl --install -d Ubuntu-24.04`. Then restart and create your user name when asked.
sections.tip: Choose a short lowercase user name without spaces; you will type it a lot.

sections.title: Snapshots: your undo button
body: A **snapshot** saves the complete state of the VM. Take one called `clean-install` right after the first successful boot and before every risky experiment. If you break something, restore the snapshot in seconds.
In VirtualBox: Machine ▸ Take Snapshot; in UTM: clone the VM or use the QEMU snapshot option. For WSL export a backup: `wsl --export Ubuntu-24.04 backup.tar`.
sections.danger: A snapshot is not a backup of your real files; if the host disk fails, snapshots are lost with it.

sections.title: Networking basics
body: **NAT** (default) lets the VM reach the internet but hides it from your network; use port forwarding to reach it. **Bridged** puts the VM on your LAN with its own IP address. **Host-only** connects only the VM and your computer.
For learning, NAT with a port-forward rule (host port 2222 → guest port 22) or bridged are both fine. Inside the VM check your address with `ip -brief a`.

commands.what: Shows interfaces with state and IP address.
commands.why: You need the IP address to connect over SSH.

sections.title: Connect with SSH
body: The VM window is clumsy. Connect from your host terminal over **SSH** instead: copy/paste works and it is how servers are managed in real life. First make sure the SSH service is running in the VM (`sudo systemctl enable --now sshd` on Rocky/Alma, `ssh` on Ubuntu).
Then from your host: `ssh user@IP` (bridged) or `ssh -p 2222 user@127.0.0.1` (NAT with port forward). Accept the host key with `yes`.

commands.where: From your host to the VM or any server.

commands.what: Creates a key pair for password-less login.
commands.why: Safer and more convenient than passwords.

commands.what: Installs your public key on the VM.

sections.tip: Take a snapshot after SSH works — it is the best state to return to.

t01.text: Warm-up: in the simulator read `cat /etc/os-release` to see what an installed system tells you.
t01.hint: The file name has a hyphen.

t02.text: Warm-up: run `id` and see your user, uid and groups (`wheel` means administrator).

t03.text: Guided: run `hostname` and then `uname -r` — the first facts to note after any installation.

t04.text: Predict: what will `sudo whoami` print? Think, then run it.
t04.hint: sudo runs the command as root.

t05.text: Debug: `cat /etc/os_release` fails. Run it, read the error, then run the correct command.

t06.text: Mini project: save the distribution name line into `~/vm-summary.txt` with `grep PRETTY_NAME /etc/os-release > ~/vm-summary.txt`.
t06.hint: `>` writes the output to a file.

t07.text: Challenge: create `~/vm-lab/snapshots` and `~/vm-lab/notes` with one `mkdir -p` command.

t08.text: TICKET #3001 — The lab needs a VM report: write hostname, kernel version and user name (in that order) into `~/vm-report.txt`, one per line.
t08.hint: First command with `>`, the next two with `>>`.

vm.intro: This is the main path of this module: work through the steps on your computer. Tick "Done" or paste an output to be checked.

v01.title: Download the ISO
v01.text: Download Rocky Linux 9 or AlmaLinux 9 (minimal ISO; ARM64 for Apple Silicon) or Ubuntu 24.04 and note the published SHA-256 value.
differs: Apple Silicon needs the aarch64/arm64 ISO; x86_64 will not boot in UTM natively.

v02.title: Verify the checksum
v02.text: Compute the SHA-256 of your ISO and paste the output. Compare it manually with the published value.

blocks.expected: (macOS) 64 hex characters followed by the file name

differs: 64 hexadecimal characters are expected; a shorter output means the command failed.
Windows: `Get-FileHash file.iso -Algorithm SHA256` prints a table; paste the Hash column.
Different from the published value? Delete the file and download again.

v03.title: Create and install the VM
v03.text: Create the VM (2 CPU, 4 GB RAM, 25 GB disk), install the system, create an administrator user and boot into the login prompt.
differs: Boot loop or "no bootable medium": check the ISO is attached and the boot order starts with the optical drive.
VirtualBox on Windows: enable virtualization (VT-x/AMD-V) in the BIOS and disable Hyper-V conflicts.

v04.title: First login
v04.text: Log in with your user and show which system you installed. Paste the output.
differs: On Ubuntu `NAME="Ubuntu"` appears; both are fine for this course.
On WSL the file exists too; the text is the same.

v05.title: Take a snapshot
v05.text: Shut down cleanly with `sudo poweroff`, take a snapshot named `clean-install`, then start the VM again.
differs: Snapshots greyed out? Power the VM off first (in VirtualBox the snapshot button is in the machine tools).

v06.title: Find the IP address
v06.text: Show your interfaces and paste the output.
differs: `10.0.2.15` means NAT; use the port-forward rule to reach it from the host.
No IPv4 address on enp0s3? Run `nmcli device` and connect the interface, or check the VM network adapter is enabled.

v07.title: Connect over SSH
v07.text: Connect from your host terminal to the VM and run the command below. Paste the output.

blocks.expected: (you get a prompt on the VM)

differs: `Connection refused`: sshd is not running (`sudo systemctl enable --now sshd`).
`Connection timed out`: wrong IP or no port-forward rule (NAT).
`Permission denied`: wrong user name or password.

v08.title: Update the system
v08.text: Bring the system up to date, reboot and tick "Done" when the update finished without errors.

blocks.cmd: sudo apt update && sudo apt -y upgrade   # Ubuntu

differs: `Could not resolve host`: the VM has no internet; check the network adapter.

q1.q: What does a matching SHA-256 checksum tell you?
options: The ISO is the newest version
The file is complete and unmodified
The ISO is free of cost
q1.explain: A checksum is a fingerprint; equal fingerprints mean the file is identical to the published one.

q2.q: Which network mode hides the VM from your LAN but allows internet access?
q2.explain: NAT shares the host connection; use port forwarding to reach the VM.

q3.q: When should you take a snapshot?
q3.explain: A snapshot is a quick undo point; take one before changes you may regret.

q4.q: Which tool is the usual choice on an Apple Silicon Mac?
q4.explain: Apple Silicon is ARM; UTM runs ARM64 guests natively.

summary: A VM is a safe, disposable Linux that you can fully control.
Always verify the ISO checksum before installing.
Snapshot after a clean install and before experiments.
SSH from the host terminal is the professional way to work.

glossary.meaning: Virtual machine: a complete computer simulated by software.
Disk image file of an installation medium.
Fingerprint of a file used to detect damage or tampering.
Saved state of a VM you can return to.
Secure Shell: encrypted remote terminal protocol.
Network address translation: VM shares the host connection.
